mainTopic: The source of the Torah's eating and drinking measures: כביצה for טומאת אוכלין, the Sinai origin of measures, and the cheekful measure for drinking on יום הכפורים
overview: A ברייתא teaches that almost every eating measure in the Torah is a כזית. The exception is טומאת אוכלין, where the measure is a כביצה, and יום הכפורים is brought as a parallel case: the פסוק says ״לא תעונה״, and the measure is a ככותבת. The גמרא first tries to learn the כביצה from 'food that comes from food,' a chicken egg. That approach runs into challenges about other foods and about bigger and smaller eggs. רבי אבהו then gives his own source: food eaten at one time, and the throat holds no more than a chicken egg. רבי אלעזר advises someone who eats חלב today to write down the amount, in case a future בית דין changes the measures, and the גמרא works out what 'increase the measures' means. רבי יוחנן teaches that the measures of punishments are הלכה למשה מסיני; the court of יעבץ only restored measures that had been forgotten. Finally, the גמרא explains the משנה's drinking measure, מלא לוגמיו, as one cheek that looks like a full mouth. It defends this reading against a ברייתא, and רב הושעיא's challenge about בית שמאי and בית הלל continues on the next amud.

steps.title: All eating measures are an olive, except impure food
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא states that every eating measure is a כזית except טומאת אוכלין, because the פסוק changed its wording, and חכמים changed the measure. The proof is יום הכפורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: All the measures are an olive-size, except for the impurity of foods. There, the verse changed its wording, and the חכמים changed the measure. The proof for this is יום הכפורים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא with a general rule: eating measures are a כזית. It names one exception, טומאת אוכלין, and points to יום הכפורים as proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic rule is that Torah eating measures are a כזית. When the פסוק uses unusual language, חכמים understood that the measure is different too. יום הכפורים is brought as a parallel case where the same thing happened.

keyTerms.meaning: Measures (the minimum amounts that matter in halacha)
Impurity of foods (how big a piece of food must be to pass on impurity)
The verse changed its expression or wording
A proof (or support) for the matter

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the principle behind the whole sugya: unusual wording in a פסוק signals an unusual measure.

phrases.english: All the measures, all of them, are an olive-size,
except for the impurity of foods,
for the verse changed its wording about them,
and the Sages changed their measure.
And the proof for this is Yom Kippur.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating measures are a כזית, except טומאת אוכלין, where the unusual wording of the פסוק led חכמים to set a different measure.

steps.title: How Yom Kippur shows changed wording and a changed measure
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the יום הכפורים example. The changed wording is ״לא תעונה״, and the changed measure is ככותבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the change in the verse's wording? 'Shall not be afflicted.' And what is the change the חכמים made in its measure? A large date-size.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what exactly changed in the יום הכפורים case and answers right away. The פסוק says "not afflicted" instead of "eats," and the measure is a ככותבת instead of a כזית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah could have said "whoever eats on יום הכפורים." Instead it says "whoever is not afflicted." So the measure is based on what stops a person from feeling afflicted: a ככותבת, which settles the mind.

keyTerms.meaning: Size of a large date, slightly less than an egg

phrases.english: What is the change of the verse's wording?
From "shall not be afflicted";
and what change did the Sages make in its measure?
A large date-size.

steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the unusual wording and the different measure are in the case of יום הכפורים.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wording is ״לא תעונה״, and the measure is ככותבת.

steps.title: Why bring Yom Kippur as extra proof?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needs the יום הכפורים example at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the point of saying 'the proof for this is יום הכפורים'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the טומאת אוכלין case alone is not enough. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא already has a case of changed wording leading to a changed measure. So why add a second case? The גמרא wants to understand what the second case adds.

keyTerms.meaning: And what (is the reason or meaning)?

phrases.english: And what is meant by "the proof for this is Yom Kippur"?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the טומאה case alone is not enough proof.

steps.title: Without Yom Kippur we would dismiss the wording as style
steps.stepSummary: From the טומאה פסוק alone, one might say the double wording is just the Torah's way of speaking. יום הכפורים shows that changed wording really teaches a halacha.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because if we learned it only from there, I would have said: that is just the style of the verse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the טומאה פסוק alone could be read as ordinary Torah style. יום הכפורים proves that such wording teaches a real change in halacha.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase ״האוכל אשר יאכל״ might look like normal Torah phrasing with no extra meaning. In יום הכפורים, the switch to "afflicted" clearly carries meaning. That shows חכמים do learn halacha from unusual wording.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have thought (an initial assumption that gets corrected)
The normal style of the verse (no extra meaning)

steps.whatToRemember: Unusual wording in a פסוק can teach a different measure. יום הכפורים proves this is a real rule and not just Torah style.

phrases.english: Because if we learned only from there,
I would have said: it is just the style of the verse.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The טומאה wording could be dismissed as style. יום הכפורים proves that changed wording means a changed halacha.

steps.title: Where do we learn the egg-size for impure food?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that the measure for טומאת אוכלין is a כביצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The impurity of foods is an egg-size — from where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question: what is the source for the exact כביצה measure? This sets up רבי אבהו's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 told us the measure is different from a כזית. It did not say what the new measure is or where it comes from. Now the גמרא asks for the specific source for an egg-size.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this?

phrases.english: Impurity of foods is an egg-size — from where do we know?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: The Scriptural source for the כביצה measure.

steps.title: Food that comes from food: a chicken egg
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו in the name of רבי אלעזר learns from ״מכל האוכל אשר יאכל״ that the measure is food that comes from food, which is a chicken egg.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי אלעזר: the verse says, 'Of all food that may be eaten.' This means food that comes from food. Which is that? A chicken egg.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו gives the source. The doubled word for food hints at "food that comes out of food," and that is a chicken egg.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra word "אוכל" is read as describing food that comes out of another food. A chicken egg comes from a chicken, which is itself food. So the measure for passing on טומאה is the size of a chicken egg.

keyTerms.meaning: "Of all food that may be eaten" (ויקרא יא:לד)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Elazar:
For the verse says: "Of all food that may be eaten" —
food that comes from food;
and which is that? A chicken egg.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר דְּאָמַר קְרָא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The doubled word ״אוכל... יאכל״ points to food from food, which is a chicken egg, so the measure is a כביצה.

steps.title: Why not a young goat?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: a kid goat also comes from food (its mother), so why not make that the measure?
steps.simpleTranslation: But say it means a young goat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אבהו. A baby goat comes from a mother goat, which is food, so it should also count as "food from food."
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the rule is simply "food that comes from food," many things could fit. A kid goat is born from an edible animal. Why pick an egg?

keyTerms.meaning: But say instead (a challenge offering another option)

phrases.english: But say it means a young goat!

steps.kashyaTarget: The identification of "food from food" as a chicken egg
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A kid goat also comes from an edible animal, so it should fit the definition too.

steps.title: A goat still needs שחיטה
steps.stepSummary: A kid goat is not yet food when born, because it needs שחיטה before it can be eaten.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is lacking slaughter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a live goat is not food yet, since it still needs שחיטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Food from food" means something that is already food when it comes out. An egg is edible right away. A goat needs שחיטה first, so it does not qualify.

phrases.english: It is lacking slaughter.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the term more precisely: it must be edible as it comes out
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A kid goat comes from food, so it should qualify.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is not food until שחיטה, so it does not qualify.

steps.title: Why not a בן פקועה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: a בן פקועה needs no שחיטה, so why not make it the measure?
steps.simpleTranslation: But say it means a בן פקועה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back with a fetus found inside a slaughtered animal. Such an animal is permitted without its own שחיטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous answer was that a goat needs שחיטה. A בן פקועה is permitted through its mother's שחיטה. So the earlier answer seems not to apply to it.

keyTerms.meaning: A fetus found alive in a slaughtered animal; it is permitted without its own שחיטה

phrases.english: But say it means a ben pekua!

steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that "food from food" must not need שחיטה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A בן פקועה needs no שחיטה yet still comes from food, so it should qualify.

steps.title: A בן פקועה still needs cutting
steps.stepSummary: Even a בן פקועה is not ready to eat. It still needs cutting, so it is not food as it is.
steps.simpleTranslation: It requires cutting.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the בן פקועה is still not ready-to-eat food. It must be cut first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not needing שחיטה is not enough. An animal still has to be cut up before it is eaten. An egg, by contrast, is food in its natural form.

phrases.english: It requires cutting.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Refining the definition: it must be fully edible as is
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A בן פקועה needs no שחיטה, so it is ready food.
steps.terutzMaskana: It still needs cutting, so only an egg is truly ready food from food.

steps.title: Why not the giant egg of a בר יוכני?
steps.stepSummary: Even granting that the measure is an egg, why a chicken egg and not the huge egg of the בר יוכני bird?
steps.simpleTranslation: But say it means the egg of the בר יוכני bird!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts that the measure is an egg but asks which egg. Why not the enormous egg of the בר יוכני?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge has moved from "what kind of food" to "what size of egg." The פסוק does not say which bird.

keyTerms.meaning: A legendary giant bird with a huge egg

phrases.english: But say it means the egg of the bar yokhani!

steps.kashyaTarget: Choosing a chicken egg as the specific egg size
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק does not specify the bird, so a much larger egg could be the measure.

steps.title: When unsure, take the smaller amount
steps.stepSummary: The rule ״תפסת מרובה לא תפסת״ means that in doubt we take the smaller, surer amount, not the huge egg.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you grabbed a lot, you didn't grab anything. If you grabbed a little, you grabbed something.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a general rule: when unsure, choose the smaller option. The smaller amount is certainly included in any larger one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah meant a big amount, the small amount is part of it anyway. So the small amount is the safe and certain reading. Choosing the huge egg rests on nothing solid.

keyTerms.meaning: If you grab a lot, you grab nothing
If you grab a little, you hold onto it

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a general interpretive rule used throughout שס: in doubt, choose the minimal reading.

phrases.english: If you grabbed a lot, you didn't grab anything;
if you grabbed a little, you grabbed something.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The measure could be the giant בר יוכני egg.
steps.terutzMaskana: In doubt we take the smaller amount, so not the giant egg.

steps.title: Then why not a tiny bird's egg?
steps.stepSummary: If we always take the smaller amount, the measure should be the egg of a very small bird, not a chicken egg.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then say it means the egg of a bird that is very small!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the last answer around. If smaller is better, a tiny bird's egg should be the measure. The גמרא gives no direct answer; instead, the next step brings a different derivation that avoids the problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule ״תפסת מועט״ seems to prove too much. It points to the smallest egg there is, not a chicken egg. The גמרא now needs another reason to land on a chicken egg.
steps.confusionAlert: This challenge is not answered on its own terms. The next step drops the 'food from food' reading and brings רבי אבהו's own source for the egg measure.

phrases.english: But say it means the egg of a bird
that is very small!

steps.kashyaTarget: Using ״תפסת מועט״ to arrive at a chicken egg
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the smaller amount is preferred, the smallest bird's egg should be the measure, not a chicken egg.

steps.title: רבי אבהו's own source: food eaten in one swallow
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו drops the earlier approach. He reads the פסוק as food eaten at one time, and the חכמים measured that the throat holds no more than a chicken egg.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו himself said: The verse says 'of all food which may be eaten.' That means food you eat at one time. The Sages estimated that the throat cannot hold more than a chicken egg.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו gives his own explanation of the egg measure. It avoids the problems the גמרא raised in the earlier steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier attempts kept running into trouble: why this egg and not a bigger or smaller one? Here the measure is not taken from a particular bird. It comes from a real limit, the amount of food a person swallows at one time, which the חכמים measured as one chicken egg.

keyTerms.meaning: At one time, in one go
And the Sages estimated or measured
The throat or esophagus, where food is swallowed

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי אבהו, the כביצה measure for food טומאה comes from 'food eaten at one time.' The throat holds no more than a chicken egg.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answers the questions from steps 11 to 13. The chicken egg was not chosen at random. It matches the real amount a person swallows at once.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abahu himself said:
phrases.notes: His own approach, different from the one argued about earlier

phrases.english: "Of all food which may be eaten"
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק in ויקרא יא:לד.

phrases.english: food that you eat at one time.
phrases.notes: Reads 'which may be eaten' as one act of eating

phrases.english: And the Sages estimated:
the throat does not hold
more than a chicken egg.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 13 by giving a new source that ties the measure to the size of one swallow.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New source and reasoning that replaces the earlier approach
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The egg measure seemed to require choosing one bird's egg over another, which raised questions about bigger and smaller eggs.
steps.terutzMaskana: The measure is one swallow of food, and the חכמים measured that as one chicken egg.

steps.title: One who eats forbidden fat should write down the amount
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר teaches that someone who eats חלב nowadays should record how much he ate, in case a later בית דין increases the measures.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: Someone who eats forbidden fat nowadays should write down the amount he ate, because another court may come and increase the measures.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the sugya is discussing measures, the גמרא brings a new teaching of רבי אלעזר. It is practical advice about recording how much forbidden fat someone ate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Today, with no בית המקדש, a person who ate חלב by mistake cannot bring his קרבן. רבי אלעזר says he should write down the exact amount, because a future בית דין might set the measures differently. The phrase 'increase the measures' is unclear, and the גמרא will ask about it next.

keyTerms.meaning: Forbidden fat of an animal. Eating it by mistake requires a קרבן חטאת
Nowadays, when there is no בית המקדש
And will increase or change the measures

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
One who eats forbidden fat nowadays
phrases.notes: Unknowingly, so he would owe a קרבן

phrases.english: must write down for himself the measure,
lest another court come
and increase the measures.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: הָאוֹכֵל חֵלֶב בִּזְמַן הַזֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic connected to the discussion of measures.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who ate חלב nowadays should record the exact amount, in case a future court changes the measures.

steps.title: What does it mean to increase the measures?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'increase the measures' means. It suggests one reading: a future court would require a קרבן even for a smaller כזית.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'increase the measures' mean? If you say it means the court will require an offering even for the size of a small olive...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what רבי אלעזר meant and offers a first possible reading. This step sets up the challenge that comes right after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One possibility is that a future court would shrink the כזית. Then a person who ate an amount smaller than today's כזית, but equal to the new smaller one, would owe a קרבן. The גמרא raises this reading only to test it in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (proposing a reading in order to test it)
That they will require an offering
A small olive's size, smaller than the current כזית

steps.confusionAlert: Under this first proposal, 'increasing the measures' would mean making the punishable amount smaller, so more cases would require a קרבן. This proposal is rejected in step 17, and step 18 gives the accepted reading: a larger כזית.

phrases.english: What does 'increase the measures' mean?
If we say that they will require an offering
for the size of a small olive,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the wording of רבי אלעזר's teaching means.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What change a future court would make by 'increasing the measures'.

steps.title: An offering is brought only if knowing would have stopped him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the small-olive reading with a ברייתא. A person brings a קרבן only if he would have stopped had he known. Someone who ate less than today's כזית would not have stopped on account of a קרבן, since no קרבן was due for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught: 'which should not be done, by mistake, and is guilty.' One who would turn back once he knows brings an offering for his mistake. One who would not turn back once he knows does not bring an offering for his mistake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to attack the reading from step 16. A קרבן is only for someone who would have turned back if he had known.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under today's rules, eating less than a full כזית does not require a קרבן. So even if the person had known exactly what he was eating, he would not have stopped. Since knowing would not have made him turn back, a later court cannot make him bring a קרבן. So the 'small olive' reading cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: One who would turn back because of his knowledge, meaning he would have stopped had he known

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a basic rule for קרבנות: a חטאת is only for a sin the person would have avoided if he had known. Whether something is a sin depends on the law at the time he did it.

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught:
"which should not be done, by mistake, and is guilty"
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק in ויקרא ד:כז.

phrases.english: one who would turn back because of his knowledge
brings an offering for his mistake.
One who would not turn back because of his knowledge
does not bring an offering for his mistake.
phrases.notes: Eating less than today's כזית brings no קרבן (though a חצי שיעור, a partial amount, is still forbidden), so knowing wouldn't have stopped him for that reason.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reading proposed in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that a future court would require a קרבן for a smaller כזית.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קרבן requires that the person would have stopped had he known. Eating less than today's כזית was allowed, so knowing would not have stopped him, and a later change cannot make him owe a קרבן.

steps.title: A future court may require a larger olive
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-reads 'increase the measures' as a future בית דין requiring a bigger כזית before a קרבן is owed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means that a future court would not obligate a קרבן until there is the amount of a large olive.
steps.whatsHappening: Because the 'smaller olive' reading was knocked down in step 17, the גמרא offers a new reading. 'Increase' means a future court might make the כזית bigger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a future בית דין says a כזית is larger, someone who ate today's כזית may turn out to have eaten less than the required amount. He would then be exempt from a חטאת. This explains why he should write down exactly how much he ate.

keyTerms.meaning: the amount of a large olive

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'increase' helps the person: a bigger measure means he may no longer owe a קרבן. It does not mean more people become obligated.

phrases.english: Rather: that they will not obligate a sacrifice
until there is the amount of a large olive.
phrases.notes: With a bigger measure, a smaller amount he ate might not count anymore.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: דְּלָא מְחַיְּיבִי קׇרְבָּן עַד דְּאִיכָּא כְּזַיִת גָּדוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the small-olive reading that step 17 rejected.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the phrase 'increase the measures'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A future court would make the כזית smaller and require more קרבנות.
steps.terutzMaskana: A future court may make the כזית larger, which could exempt someone from a קרבן.

steps.title: How did the first reading explain the word 'increase'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back and asks how the original small-olive idea could have fit the word 'increase.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to what we first thought, that they would obligate a קרבן for a small olive, what does 'increase the measures' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the first idea for a moment. It asks why רבי אלעזר would say 'increase' if he meant a smaller measure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A smaller כזית sounds like 'decreasing' the measure, not increasing it. So the wording seemed to contradict the first reading. The גמרא wants to show how that reading could have understood the word.

keyTerms.meaning: it entered our mind; we initially assumed
the amount of a small olive

phrases.english: And according to what entered our mind at first,
that they would obligate a sacrifice for a small olive,
what is the meaning of 'will increase the measures'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the reading from step 16 to check its wording.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the word 'increase' fits a ruling that makes the measure smaller.

steps.title: More offerings because of the measures
steps.stepSummary: 'Increase' could mean that the number of קרבנות goes up because of a smaller measure.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps the court will increase the number of offerings because of the measures.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question in step 19. 'Increase' refers to the number of קרבנות, not to the size of the measure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A smaller כזית means more people become obligated, so more קרבנות are brought. Read this way, 'increase the measures' is shorthand for 'increase offerings because of the measures.'

phrases.english: Perhaps he will increase the offerings
because of the measures.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question from step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Increase' means more קרבנות are brought because of the smaller measure.

steps.title: Measures and punishments come from Sinai
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that measures and punishments are הלכה למשה מסיני.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Measures and punishments are a law given to משה at Sinai.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement opens a related topic: where the Torah's measures come from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since we were just talking about courts changing measures, the גמרא brings רבי יוחנן's teaching about their source. As quoted here, he lists both 'measures' and 'punishments' as oral laws from Sinai. That wording is about to be challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: set measures, such as a כְּזַיִת
an oral law given to משה at Sinai

steps.whyThisMatters: It establishes that the Torah's measures are ancient and binding. They are not inventions of later courts.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Measures and punishments
are a law to Moshe from Sinai.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: שִׁיעוּרִין וָעוֹנָשִׁין הֲלָכָה לְמֹשֶׁה מִסִּינַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connected topic: the source of the measures discussed in steps 15-20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Measures and punishments are הלכה למשה מסיני.

steps.title: Punishments are written in the Torah
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that punishments are written in the Torah, so they cannot be an oral law.
steps.simpleTranslation: Punishments are written explicitly in the Torah!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A הלכה למשה מסיני is a law passed down orally, not written in the פסוקים. Punishments like מלקות and כרת are spelled out in the Torah. So calling them 'from Sinai' orally makes no sense.

phrases.english: Punishments are explicitly written!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word 'punishments' in רבי יוחנן's statement.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Something written in the Torah cannot be described as an oral law from Sinai.

steps.title: The measures for punishments are from Sinai
steps.stepSummary: The statement is re-read: the measures that make a person liable to punishment are from Sinai.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what he meant: רבי יוחנן said, the measures of punishments are a law to משה from Sinai.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording. רבי יוחנן was not talking about two separate things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The punishments themselves are written in the Torah. What comes orally from Sinai is how much a person must do to be punished, such as a כזית of forbidden food. 'Measures and punishments' becomes 'measures of punishments.'

keyTerms.meaning: the measures that make one liable to punishment

phrases.english: Rather, this is what he said:
(Rabbi Yochanan said:)
The measures of punishments
are a law to Moshe from Sinai.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 22.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Measures and punishments are two separate oral laws.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the measures that create liability for punishment are from Sinai.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the same corrected idea.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way: The measures of punishments are a law to משה from Sinai.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that matches רבי יוחנן's corrected statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא uses the exact wording 'measures of punishments.' This confirms that the correction in step 23 is right.

keyTerms.meaning: it was also taught this way in a ברייתא

phrases.english: It was also taught so:
The measures of punishments
are a law to Moshe from Sinai.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 23.
steps.raayaObject: The measures of punishments are הלכה למשה מסיני.

steps.title: The court of יעבץ set the measures
steps.stepSummary: 'Others' say the court of יעבץ instituted the measures.
steps.simpleTranslation: Others say: The court of יעבץ established them.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a second opinion about where the measures came from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This view seems to credit a later court, the court of יעבץ, with creating the measures. That would contradict the idea that they come from Sinai. The גמרא challenges it next.

keyTerms.meaning: the court of יעבץ (identified with עתניאל בן קנז)

phrases.english: Others say:
The court of Yaavetz established them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲחֵרִים אוֹמְרִים: בֵּית דִּינוֹ שֶׁל יַעְבֵּץ תִּיקְּנוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second opinion within the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The court of יעבץ instituted the measures.

steps.title: A נביא may not add new laws
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: the Torah says 'these are the מצוות,' so no נביא may introduce something new.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written, 'These are the מצוות,' which teaches that a נביא is not allowed to introduce anything new from now on!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the view that the court of יעבץ created the measures.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק 'אלה המצות' teaches that the Torah's laws were complete at Sinai. No later נביא may add to them. So how could the court of יעבץ have made up the measures?

phrases.english: But it is written: 'These are the commandments,'
that a prophet is not permitted
to introduce anything new from now on!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the view in step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the court of יעבץ established the measures.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק forbids any נביא from adding new Torah law after Sinai.

steps.title: Forgotten and then restored
steps.stepSummary: The measures were forgotten, and the court of יעבץ re-established them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, they forgot them, and they went back and re-established them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge. The court of יעבץ did not invent the measures. It restored them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The measures came from Sinai but were forgotten over time. The court of יעבץ brought them back. So both opinions agree on the Sinai source, and nothing new was added.
steps.whatToRemember: The measures that create liability, like a כזית, are הלכה למשה מסיני. Even the view crediting the court of יעבץ means they only restored forgotten laws. They did not create new ones.

phrases.english: Rather, they forgot them
and they went back and re-established them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 26.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The court of יעבץ invented the measures.
steps.terutzMaskana: The court of יעבץ restored measures from Sinai that had been forgotten.

steps.title: שמואל defines the drinking measure as one cheek that looks like a full mouth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's drinking measure. רב יהודה, quoting שמואל, explains that it means an amount that looks like a full mouth when pushed to one side.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: one who drinks a cheekful is liable. רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: this does not mean actually both cheeks full. It means any amount that, if pushed to one side of the mouth, would look like a full mouth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic from the משנה, the measure for drinking on יום כיפור. שמואל explains what 'מלא לוגמיו' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read literally, 'מלא לוגמיו' sounds like both cheeks completely full. שמואל makes the amount smaller: one cheek's worth is enough, because from the side it looks like a full mouth. This smaller amount is the basis for everything that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: A cheekful, literally 'the fullness of his cheeks'
He pushes it to one side of the mouth

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical amount of drinking that makes a person liable on יום כיפור, and it depends on how much a person's cheek holds.

phrases.english: One who drinks a cheekful (is liable).
Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
Not actually a full (two-)cheekful,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא כׇּל שֶׁאִילּוּ יְסַלְּקֶנּוּ לְצַד אֶחָד
phrases.english: rather, any amount that, if he pushed it to one side,
would look like a full cheekful.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: לֹא מְלֹא לוּגְמָיו מַמָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה to start a new topic, the drinking measure, after the general discussion of where the measures of punishments come from (steps 21-27).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The drinking measure is one cheek's worth that looks like a full mouth when pushed to one side, not both cheeks literally full.

steps.title: The משנה's wording seems to mean a real cheekful
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the משנה plainly says 'מלא לוגמיו,' a real cheekful.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in the משנה: 'a cheekful'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל by pointing to the plain words of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says 'a cheekful,' not 'like a cheekful.' שמואל's 'looks like' reading seems to add something the text does not say.

phrases.english: But we learned: 'a cheekful'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks שמואל's definition from Step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's definition of the measure as 'looks like a cheekful'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The plain wording of the משנה means a real, full cheekful.

steps.title: Read the משנה as 'like a cheekful'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה should be read as 'like a cheekful.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: 'like a cheekful.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by adjusting how we read the משנה so that it fits שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reading the words as 'like a cheekful' means the amount only has to look like a full mouth. That matches שמואל's one-cheek measure.

keyTerms.meaning: Like a cheekful, an amount that looks like a full mouth

phrases.english: Say: 'like a cheekful.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of Step 29.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה requires literally both cheeks full.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה means an amount that looks like a full mouth, as שמואל said.

steps.title: A ברייתא has בית הלל say 'a cheekful' as a separate view from 'like a cheekful'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites a ברייתא listing four opinions. In it, בית הלל say 'a cheekful,' while רבי אליעזר says 'like a cheekful,' so the two seem to be different amounts.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: How much must one drink to be liable? בית שמאי say: a רביעית. בית הלל say: a cheekful. רבי יהודה says in the name of רבי אליעזר: like a cheekful. רבי יהודה בן בתירא says: the amount of one swallow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל from a ברייתא. In it, בית הלל's 'a cheekful' is listed separately from רבי אליעזר's 'like a cheekful.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'like a cheekful' is רבי אליעזר's separate view, then בית הלל's 'a cheekful' must mean a real cheekful. Since the halacha follows בית הלל, this seems to go against שמואל's smaller, 'looks like' measure.

keyTerms.meaning: A quarter-לוג, a set liquid measure

steps.confusionAlert: The phrase 'כמלא לוגמיו' that the גמרא used to defend שמואל in Step 30 appears here as רבי אליעזר's separate opinion. That is exactly the problem.

phrases.english: They challenged: How much must one drink to be liable?
Beit Shammai say: a quarter-log,
and Beit Hillel say: a cheekful.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר: כִּמְלֹא לוּגְמָיו.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: like a cheekful.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא אוֹמֵר: כְּדֵי גְמִיעָה.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says: the amount of a swallow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the answer in Step 30, brings a stronger challenge to שמואל from a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא separates בית הלל ('a cheekful') from רבי אליעזר ('like a cheekful'), so בית הלל must mean a real cheekful.

steps.title: Read the ברייתא the same way as the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is no stronger than the משנה. Just as the משנה was read as 'looks like,' בית הלל in the ברייתא can be read that way too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is the ברייתא better than the משנה? Just as we explained the משנה to mean 'so that it looks like a cheekful,' here too it means 'so that it looks like a cheekful.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by applying to the ברייתא the same reading it already gave the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא uses the same words as the משנה, 'מלא לוגמיו.' If those words in the משנה can mean 'looks like a cheekful,' the same words in the ברייתא can too, so בית הלל agree with שמואל.

phrases.english: Is it better than our Mishnah,
which we explained as 'so that it looks like'?
Here too, 'so that it looks like'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the ברייתא challenge of Step 31 by reusing the reading from Step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Same re-reading applied to a parallel source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's בית הלל mean a real cheekful.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא's בית הלל also mean 'looks like a cheekful.'

steps.title: Then בית הלל and רבי אליעזר would say the same thing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that if בית הלל mean 'looks like a cheekful,' their view is the same as רבי אליעזר's.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, that is the same as רבי אליעזר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave: it seems to erase the difference between two opinions in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא would not list the same opinion twice. If בית הלל and רבי אליעזר both mean 'looks like a cheekful,' there is no reason to quote רבי אליעזר separately.

phrases.english: If so, that is the same as Rabbi Eliezer!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of Step 32.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading בית הלל in the ברייתא as 'looks like a cheekful'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under that reading, בית הלל and רבי אליעזר hold the same view, which makes the separate listing pointless.

steps.title: They differ over a 'tight' cheekful
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that בית הלל and רבי אליעזר differ over a slightly-less-than-full cheekful.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is a 'tight' cheekful.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by naming a small case where the two opinions give different results.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A 'tight cheekful' is one cheek that is almost, but not quite, full. According to בית הלל you need a complete one-cheek amount. According to רבי אליעזר even this slightly smaller amount makes you liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Tight, scant, slightly less than full

phrases.english: The difference between them is a scant (tight) cheekful.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of Step 33.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: בית הלל and רבי אליעזר hold the same measure.
steps.terutzMaskana: בית הלל require a full one-cheek amount. רבי אליעזר is satisfied with a slightly smaller, scant cheekful.

steps.title: רב הושעיא: this would make בית הלל stricter than בית שמאי
steps.stepSummary: רב הושעיא objects that a one-cheek measure is smaller than a רביעית. That would make this a case where בית הלל are stricter than בית שמאי, yet it is not on the known list of such cases. The answer begins with 'he said to him.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הושעיא challenged this: If so, this would be one of the leniencies of בית שמאי and the stringencies of בית הלל! He said to him:
steps.whatsHappening: רב הושעיא raises a strong objection to treating בית הלל's measure as a single cheek. The last words, 'he said to him,' set up the answer that continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A one-cheek amount is less than a רביעית, so בית הלל would make a person liable sooner than בית שמאי. That makes בית הלל the stricter side here. Cases where בית שמאי are lenient and בית הלל strict are specially listed in מסכת עדיות, and this case is not on that list.

keyTerms.term: מִקּוּלֵּי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּמֵחוּמְרֵי בֵּית הִלֵּל
keyTerms.meaning: Among the cases where בית שמאי are lenient and בית הלל are strict

steps.confusionAlert: Usually בית שמאי are the strict side. The problem here is that this case would be one of the rare exceptions, and those exceptions are all listed in מסכת עדיות.

phrases.english: Rav Hoshaya strongly objected to it:
If so, it would be

phrases.aramaic: מִקּוּלֵּי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּמֵחוּמְרֵי בֵּית הִלֵּל!
phrases.english: among the leniencies of Beit Shammai and the stringencies of Beit Hillel!
He said to him:
phrases.notes: Opens the answer, which continues on the next amud

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the whole one-cheek reading of בית הלל built in Steps 28 to 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading בית הלל's measure as a single cheekful, smaller than a רביעית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reading makes בית הלל stricter than בית שמאי, but this case is missing from the list in מסכת עדיות of all such cases.
